title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the shortened pattern, the affirmative any and the evidence

questions.prompt: The reading club of Bizerte is printing a line on its bookmarks. The line has to say, in the shortest correct English there is, that an evening is better when more people come. Which line does the club print?

options.text: The most, the merriest.
More is merrier.
The more, the merrier.
The more merrier.

questions.explanation: "The more, the merrier." is the printed form: when the two halves of a parallel change would contain nothing but the verb be and its subject, English drops them and leaves the two comparatives standing, each with its own the. "The most, the merriest." replaces both comparatives by superlatives, and a superlative ranks one thing above all the others instead of tying two changes together. "More is merrier." throws away both the, which are the two words that hold the halves together, and puts a verb back where the shortened form has none. And "The more merrier." keeps one the for two comparatives and so joins them into a single phrase, leaving nothing being compared with anything.

questions.prompt: A guide is being written for a school open day in Monastir. Its author wants one sentence meaning this: it does not matter which pupil a visitor asks, every one of them will be able to show the way to the reading room. Which sentence carries that meaning?

options.text: Some pupil will show you the reading room.
Any pupil will show you the reading room.
Anybody will not show you the reading room.
No pupil will show you the reading room.

questions.explanation: "Any pupil will show you the reading room." carries it exactly: inside an affirmative statement, any is not asking whether such a pupil exists, it means practically every one, so take whichever pupil you like and the sentence still holds. "Some pupil will show you the reading room." points at one particular pupil the writer cannot name, which is the opposite of it does not matter which. "No pupil will show you the reading room." says the visitor will be helped by nobody at all. And "Anybody will not show you the reading room." pushes an any- word in front of a negative verb, a place English never gives it; when the sentence is negative the negative comes first, nobody will show you.

questions.prompt: Read this short piece from a regional paper, then answer. "Ten years ago the Gafsa music fair sold tickets only at its own gate. This year it sold seven out of ten before the gates opened, most of them from a telephone. Its director says the fair now spends more on its website than on posters, and that the two evenings it added in 2024 were both full." The director claims that the fair no longer needs its posters as much as it once did. Which detail of the piece supports that claim most directly?

options.text: The fair now spends more on its website than on posters.
Seven tickets out of ten were sold before the gates opened.
The fair added two evenings in 2024 and both were full.
The fair sold tickets only at its own gate ten years ago.

questions.explanation: "The fair now spends more on its website than on posters." is the supporting detail, because it is the only line that weighs the posters against something else, and a claim about posters needs a fact in which posters appear. "Seven tickets out of ten were sold before the gates opened." proves that selling early works, but it names no channel, so it says nothing about posters one way or the other. "The fair added two evenings in 2024 and both were full." shows that the fair is bigger than it was, which is a different claim altogether. And "The fair sold tickets only at its own gate ten years ago." describes the old arrangement; it sets the scene without measuring anything about today.

questions.prompt: A record shop notes two figures every month: the price it asks for a single, and the number of singles it sells. Its owner has noticed that whenever the price goes up, the number sold goes down. Which single sentence states that rule?

options.text: The higher the price, the less singles the shop sells.
The highest the price, the fewest singles the shop sells.
The more high the price, the fewer singles the shop sells.
The higher the price, the fewer singles the shop sells.

questions.explanation: "The higher the price, the fewer singles the shop sells." states the rule: parallel change ties two movements together and never says they must go the same way, so the first half may rise while the second falls, as long as both keep the and a comparative. "The higher the price, the less singles the shop sells." chooses the wrong comparative of quantity: singles are counted one by one, and a countable plural takes fewer, while less belongs to what cannot be counted, less money, less noise. "The highest the price, the fewest singles the shop sells." replaces both comparatives by superlatives, which rank one item above the rest instead of linking two changes. And "The more high the price, the fewer singles the shop sells." builds the comparative of a short adjective with more, where high takes -er.

questions.prompt: A journalist has written two sentences about the same market and has to choose one noun for each gap. Sentence 1: "Sales fell slowly and steadily over eight years: a long, quiet ___." Sentence 2: "In the week that followed the news, sales fell by half: a ___ nobody had expected." Which noun belongs in the second gap?

options.text: decline
era
plunge
supremacy

questions.explanation: "plunge" belongs in the second gap: a plunge is a fall that is sudden and steep, and half the sales lost inside a single week is exactly that. "decline" is the noun the first gap wants, a fall that is slow and steady and spread over years, which is why the journalist wrote long and quiet in front of it. "era" names a long period of history and not a movement of figures at all, so no fall can be one. And "supremacy" names the position of being above everybody else, which is what a market leader holds, the very opposite of a drop in sales.

questions.prompt: Four lines from a magazine article use words of this theme. Three of them build the word into a construction English allows. In which line is the word built wrongly?

options.text: The old reading room is the lifeblood of the whole club.
The company decided to blame on the radio stations for its losses.
The town wants to pay tribute to its first librarian.
Half the village could not read, and the school set out to fight that illiteracy.

questions.explanation: "The company decided to blame on the radio stations for its losses." is built wrongly: blame takes as its direct object whoever is held responsible, so the line needs to blame the radio stations for its losses. The shape with on does exist in English, but only the other way round, with the thing first, to blame its losses on the radio stations; this line has borrowed half of each. The three others are built as English builds them. "The old reading room is the lifeblood of the whole club." keeps of after lifeblood, which is a noun. "The town wants to pay tribute to its first librarian." keeps to before the person being honoured, and that to is part of the expression. And "Half the village could not read, and the school set out to fight that illiteracy." uses the noun English forms from literacy by putting the negative prefix in front of it.
